summary: Specifies changes to the Policy Core Information Model from RFC 3060. It introduces entirely new elements, such as classes for header filtering, and deprecates some existing ones, such as policy rule priorities, replacing them with better alternatives.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3460 adds to the Policy Core Information Model, the data model that describes how network policy is written down. It lets rules be nested inside other rules, gives each group of rules an explicit way of deciding which ones act, connects roles to the devices they describe, and adds variables, values and packet filters so that a rule can test a packet's header fields.

subtitle: Extensions to the Policy Core Information Model: reusable and nested rules, decision strategies, roles, variables and values, and packet filters.

tldr.problem: The Policy Core Information Model of RFC 3060 describes how policy rules are written down, but it does not cover much that real deployments need. There is no way to say which rules win when several match, no way to tie a rule to the devices it should apply to, no way to build one rule out of reusable pieces, and no way to filter packets on their header fields.
tldr.mechanism: This memo extends the model with new classes and associations. PolicyGroup and PolicyRule gain a common parent, PolicySet, which carries a decision strategy and a list of roles. A new containment relationship, PolicySetComponent, allows rules inside rules and carries the priority. New classes cover compound conditions and actions, variables and values, and two kinds of packet filter.
tldr.outcome: The extensions update RFC 3060 while keeping interoperability with implementations of the original model as far as possible. Where an original element is replaced, the old one is explicitly marked as deprecated and named against its replacement, so an implementation can tell which is which.

today: RFC 3460 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level. It updates RFC 3060, the Policy Core Information Model, and has not been obsoleted. It adds reusable and nested rules, decision strategies, roles tied to resources, variables and values, and packet filter classes to the model.

sections.title: What the Memo Changes
sections.content:
RFC 3460 specifies a number of changes to the Policy Core Information Model (PCIM) of RFC 3060. Two kinds of change are included. First, several completely new elements are introduced, for example classes for header filtering, which extend PCIM into areas it did not previously cover. Second, there are cases where elements of PCIM, for example policy rule priorities, are deprecated and replacement elements are defined, in this case priorities tied to the associations that refer to policy rules. Both kinds of change are made so that, to the extent possible, interoperability with implementations of the original PCIM model is preserved.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHOULD and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

The memo also says how the changes are made. The Policy Core Information Model is closely aligned with the DMTF's CIM Core Policy model, and since there is no separately documented set of rules for specifying IETF information models such as PCIM, it is reasonable to look to the CIM specifications for guidance on how to modify and extend a model. The rules it lists are that properties may be added to existing classes; that classes and individual properties may be marked as deprecated, with a replacement feature identified explicitly or the notation "No value" used when there is none, in this document written as DEPRECATED FOR a feature name; that classes may be inserted into the inheritance hierarchy above existing classes, with properties pulled up into the new classes, so that the existing classes keep exactly the properties they had but inherit them rather than defining them; and that new subclasses may be defined below existing classes. Everything said about classes in those rules applies to association classes, including aggregations, as well as to non-association classes.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo changes a data model, not a protocol. It adds new classes, retires old ones with a named replacement, and rearranges the class hierarchy so that new properties are inherited rather than copied.

sections.title: The List of Changes
sections.content:
The memo lists its changes in two places. The first is a short list of eight items. The PolicyRepository class and its associations are deprecated and replaced. The ways that policy rules and policy groups are aggregated are clarified and expanded. The way prioritization for policy rules is represented changes, and administrator-specified decision strategies for rule evaluation are introduced. The role of policy roles is expanded, and a means of associating a policy role with a resource is introduced. Compound policy conditions and compound policy actions are introduced. Variables and values are introduced. Variable and value subclasses for packet header filtering are introduced. Classes for device-level packet header filtering are introduced.

The second list explains each change in more detail, and in several cases notes where the change came from, which is usually the QoS policy information model, the IPsec configuration policy model, or the QoS diffserv policy model.

The PolicyRepository class becomes ReusablePolicyContainer, because the name PolicyRepository is already used in the four-box policy framework picture for the place from which the policy decision point retrieves all policy specifications, and confusing the class with that component is unhelpful. In PCIM the only associations defined for a PolicyRepository were for it to contain reusable policy conditions and actions; in PCIMe the associations for the new class are broadened so that it can contain any reusable policy element, which is why a single higher-level association replaces the two old ones.

The aggregations PolicyRuleInPolicyRule and PolicyGroupInPolicyRule have been imported from the QoS policy information model in effect, because those two aggregations and PCIM's two aggregations PolicyGroupInPolicyGroup and PolicyRuleInPolicyGroup are all combined into a single aggregation, PolicySetComponent. These aggregations make it possible to define larger chunks of reusable policy to place in a ReusablePolicyContainer, and they introduce new semantics representing the contextual implications of having one policy rule executing within the scope of another.

Compound policy conditions and compound policy actions also come from the QoS policy information model, with the concept broadened to include a parallel compound action. In both cases the idea is to create reusable chunks of policy that can exist as named elements in a ReusablePolicyContainer, and the compound classes and their associations incorporate the condition and action semantics that PCIM defined at the policy rule level, which is disjunctive normal form and conjunctive normal form for conditions and ordering for actions. Compound conditions and actions are defined to work with any component conditions and actions, so while the components may be instances of SimplePolicyCondition and SimplePolicyAction, they need not be.

The SimplePolicyCondition, PolicyVariable and PolicyValue structure is imported from the QoS policy information model, along with a list of PCIMe-level variables and a list of PCIMe-level values. Other variables and values may be defined in submodels of PCIMe if necessary, as the QoS policy information model does with a set of implicit variables corresponding to fields in RSVP flows. A corresponding SimplePolicyAction, PolicyVariable and PolicyValue structure is also defined, with the difference that the semantics of a simple condition are variable matches value while a simple action sets a variable to a value.
sections.plainLanguage: In short: the memo retires the policy repository class, lets rules and groups contain other rules and groups, moves priorities onto the containment relationship, adds a way to say which matching rule wins, ties roles to resources, adds compound conditions and actions, adds variables and values, and adds two kinds of packet filter.

sections.title: The Updated Class Hierarchy
sections.content:
Class and association hierarchies are given as two figures, with the changes from PCIM noted in parentheses. A new abstract class, PolicySet, is inserted into the inheritance hierarchy above both PolicyGroup and PolicyRule, which reflects the additional structural flexibility and semantic capability of the two subclasses. PolicySet carries two properties: PolicyDecisionStrategy, which defines the evaluation relationship among the rules in the set, and PolicyRoles, which characterizes the resources the set applies to.

Under PolicyCondition, the new SimplePolicyCondition and CompoundPolicyCondition classes are added, with CompoundFilterCondition below the latter. Under PolicyAction, SimplePolicyAction and CompoundPolicyAction are added. Two new abstract classes, PolicyVariable and PolicyValue, are added under Policy, with PolicyExplicitVariable and PolicyImplicitVariable below the former, and a subtree of specific variables and values below the latter.

The other half of the hierarchy extends the managed element side. A new class, PolicyRoleCollection, is derived from the CIM Collection class, and it appears in the same diagram as the new ReusablePolicyContainer, which is derived from AdminDomain and replaces the deprecated PolicyRepository. The new abstract class FilterEntryBase appears under System, with IpHeadersFilter and 8021Filter below it, and the new class FilterList beside them.

The association class hierarchy changes in the same way. The containment relationship between policy sets is now the single aggregation PolicySetComponent, which replaces the two PCIM aggregations PolicyGroupInPolicyGroup and PolicyRuleInPolicyGroup, so those are deprecated. The relationship of a policy set to an administrative domain or another administrative scoping system, for example a computer system, is the new abstract association PolicySetInSystem, derived from PolicyInSystem, and the PolicyGroupInSystem and PolicyRuleInSystem associations now derive from it instead of directly from PolicyInSystem.
sections.plainLanguage: The figures show where the new pieces sit. A new class called PolicySet sits above both policy groups and policy rules and holds the decision strategy and the roles. New classes for simple and compound conditions and actions, and for variables and values, hang off the existing policy classes. On the management side, a new container class replaces the old repository, and a new branch holds the packet filter classes.

sections.title: Nested Policy Rules
sections.content:
Policy is described by a set of policy rules that may be grouped into subsets. This section introduces nested rules, also called sub-rules, which are rules defined within rules, represented by the PolicySetComponent aggregation.

The relationship between a rule and its sub-rules is defined as follows. The parent rule's condition clause is a condition for evaluation of all nested rules, that is, the conditions of the parent are logically ANDed to the conditions of the sub-rules, and if the parent rule's condition clause evaluates to FALSE, sub-rules may be skipped since they also evaluate to FALSE. If the parent rule's condition evaluates to TRUE, the set of sub-rules is evaluated according to the decision strategy and priorities of Section 5.5. If the parent rule's condition evaluates to TRUE, the parent rule's set of actions is executed before the sub-rules' actions.

Parent actions are not to be confused with default actions. A default action is one that is to be executed only if none of the more specific sub-rules are executed, and if a default action needs to be specified it has to be defined as an action that is part of a catchall sub-rule associated with the parent rule, with the association linking it given the lowest priority relative to all other sub-rule associations. Such a default action works as a default when FirstMatching decision strategies are in effect; if AllMatching applies, the default action is always performed.

Policy rules have a context in which they are executed. The rule engine evaluates and applies the policy rules in the context of the managed resources identified by the policy roles, or by an explicit association. Submodels may add additional context based on rule structure, and any such context is defined by the semantics of the action classes of the submodel.

The memo gives the motivation. Rule nesting enhances policy readability, expressiveness and reusability, and is important for manageability and scalability because it lets complex rules be built from several simpler ones. It eases the task of policy management tools, because rules can be expressed in a way closer to how people think.

Nesting does not specify or require any particular order of evaluation of the conditions. Optimization of rule evaluation can be done in the decision point or the enforcement point by dedicated code, in the same way that an optimizer can produce better machine code than a programmer's own source-level optimization. If there is no optimization, the administrator writing the policy may influence evaluation through the nesting. Nested rules are not designed for policy repository retrieval optimization: it is assumed that all rules and groups assigned to a role are retrieved and enforced, and reducing the number of rules retrieved should be done by clever selection of roles.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule can contain other rules. The outer rule's condition has to be true before the inner ones are looked at, and the outer rule's actions run first. A catchall sub-rule with the lowest priority gives the default behaviour. Nesting exists to make policy easier to read and to build from reusable pieces, not to make evaluation faster.

sections.title: Priorities and Decision Strategies
sections.content:
A decision strategy specifies the evaluation method for the policies in a policy set, and two are defined. FirstMatching causes the evaluation of the rules in a set such that the only actions enforced on a given examination of the set are those of the first rule, that is the rule with the highest priority, whose conditions evaluate to TRUE. AllMatching causes the evaluation of all rules in a set, and for all of the rules whose conditions evaluate to TRUE the actions are enforced. Implementations must support FirstMatching and may support AllMatching.

Either subclass of PolicySet may contain policy sets of either subclass. Loops, including the degenerate case of a policy set that contains itself, are not allowed. The relative priority within a policy set is established by the Priority property of the PolicySetComponent aggregation of the contained instances, and the use of PCIM's PolicyRule Priority property is deprecated in favour of it. The separation has two advantages: it generalizes the concept of priority so that it can be used for both groups and rules, and it places the priority on the relationship between the parent policy set and the subordinate one, so that a priority value is used only in relation to other priorities in the same set.

Together, the decision strategy and the priority determine the processing of the rules in a set. The larger priority value represents the higher priority, and, unlike the earlier definition, the priority must have a unique value when compared with the others defined for the same aggregating policy set, so that the evaluation of rules within a set is deterministically specified.

With FirstMatching, the first rule in the set that evaluates to TRUE is the only rule whose actions are enforced. With AllMatching, all of the matching rules are enforced, and the relative priority is used to determine the order in which the actions are executed by the enforcement point, with the actions of the higher priority rules executed first. Because the higher priority rules run first, lower priority rules that also match get the last word and can produce a counter-intuitive result: if two rules both evaluate to TRUE, and the higher priority rule sets the DSCP to 3 while the lower priority rule sets the DSCP to 4, the action of the lower priority rule runs later and wins, setting the DSCP to 4. Conflicts between rules are therefore resolved by execution order.

An implementation of the rule engine need not provide the action sequencing itself, but the actions must be sequenced by the enforcement point or the decision point on its behalf.

Policy sets may be nested arbitrarily, and for a FirstMatching strategy on a policy set, any contained policy set that matches satisfies the termination criteria. A policy set is considered to match if it is a policy rule whose conditions evaluate to TRUE, or if it is a policy group and at least one of its contained groups or rules matches. The priority associated with contained policy sets then determines when evaluation of the structured set of rules stops. The memo's worked example sets out a group with a FirstMatching strategy containing a rule at priority 6, a group at priority 5 with an AllMatching strategy, and a rule at priority 4 with a FirstMatching strategy, with further nesting inside each. If the conditions of the top rule match, its actions are enforced and evaluation stops. If it does not match, the group at priority 5 is evaluated with an AllMatching strategy, and if any of the sub-rules in its subtrees evaluate to TRUE then the rule at priority 4 is not evaluated, because the FirstMatching strategy of the outer group has been satisfied. If neither yields a match, the rule at priority 4 is evaluated, and because it is FirstMatching its own children are evaluated until the first match.

Side effects. The rule engine need not be implemented as a procedural language interpreter. Any side effects of condition evaluation or of the execution of actions must not affect the result of the evaluation of other conditions evaluated in the same evaluation pass, so an implementation may evaluate all conditions in any order before applying the priority. For both decision strategies, and for the nesting of rules within rules where the actions of more than one rule may be enforced, any side effects of the enforcement of actions must not be included in condition evaluation on the same pass.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group of rules says how it is evaluated. With FirstMatching, only the highest-priority rule whose condition is true acts, and every implementation must support that. With AllMatching, every rule whose condition is true acts, higher priority first, so a lower priority rule can end up overriding a higher one. Within a group, no two rules may share a priority value, so the outcome is the same everywhere.

sections.title: Policy Roles
sections.content:
A policy role is defined in the policy terminology document as an administratively specified characteristic of a managed element, for example an interface. It is a selector for policy rules and provisioning classes, used to determine the applicability of a rule to a particular managed element.

In PCIMe, PolicyRoles is a property of PolicySet, so it is inherited by both policy rules and policy groups. The memo also adds PolicyRole as the identifying name of a collection of resources, the new class PolicyRoleCollection, where each element in the collection has the specified role characteristic.

The memo compares this with the roles in the SNMP configuration policy MIB. There, policy rules take the form of a policy filter and a policy action, where the filter is a set of conditions that determine whether the policy applies to an object instance, and can compare SNMP variables already defined in MIBs. A Role table there associates roles with elements, so elements can be filtered on their roles. The approach differs from PCIM in two ways. In PCIM a set of roles is associated with a policy rule as the values of its PolicyRoles property, and the semantics of roles are expected to be implemented by the decision point, so policies are applied to the elements with the appropriate roles. In the SNMP configuration model, no special processing is required, because roles are treated as any other SNMP variable and comparisons of role values can be included in the policy filter. And in PCIM there is no formally defined way of associating a role with an object instance, while the Role tables do exactly that.

PCIMe therefore adds the class PolicyRoleCollection, derived from the CIM Collection class. Resources that share a common role are aggregated by a PolicyRoleCollection instance through the ElementInPolicyRoleCollection aggregation, and the role is given in the PolicyRole property of the aggregating instance. A PolicyRoleCollection always exists in the context of a system, and the association PolicyRoleCollectionInSystem captures that, as was done in PCIM for policy rules and policy groups. The association between a collection and a system should be consistent with the associations that scope the policy rules and groups applied to the resources in the collection.

The memo's example: a network has 20 traffic trunks, and the administrator wants three of them to provide a gold service, with several policy rules that specify how the gold service is delivered and a PolicyRoles property set to Gold Service. To associate the three trunks with that role, an instance of PolicyRoleCollection is created with its PolicyRole property also set to Gold Service, and the three trunks are associated with it, which lets the decision point determine that the Gold Service policy rules apply to those three trunks.

Roles are used to optimize policy retrieval. It is not mandatory to implement roles or, if they are implemented, to group elements in a PolicyRoleCollection. If roles are used, then either the collection approach should be implemented or elements should be able to report their pre-programmed roles, as is done in COPS.

In PCIM, roles are only associated with policy rules, but it may be desirable to associate roles with groups of rules, for instance a group of rules that apply only to Ethernet interfaces. A policy group can be defined with a role combination of Ethernet and all the relevant rules placed in that group, and every rule in the group then implicitly inherits the role combination from the containing group, with a similar implicit inheritance applying to nested groups. There is no explicit copying of roles from container to contained entity, so this implicit inheritance leads to the possibility of defining inconsistent roles, and the handling of such inconsistencies is beyond the scope of PCIMe.
sections.plainLanguage: A role is a label an administrator puts on a device or an interface, such as Ethernet, and policy rules then apply to everything carrying that label. PCIM had no way to say which devices have a role, so the memo adds a class that collects the resources sharing a role. Groups of rules can also carry roles, and the rules inside inherit them.

sections.title: Variables, Values and Packet Filters
sections.content:
The SimplePolicyCondition class models elementary Boolean expressions of the form variable MATCH value. The MATCH relationship is implicit in the model, and its interpretation depends on the variable and the value. Arbitrarily complex Boolean expressions can be formed by chaining simple conditions with relational operators, and individual simple conditions can be negated, while complex expressions are modeled by the CompoundPolicyCondition class. The example given is SourcePort equals 80, where SourcePort is a variable, the equality operator is the relational operator generalized to a MATCH relationship, and 80 is an integer value. The complete interpretation of a simple condition depends on the binding of the variable.

Composing a simple condition requires that the ValueTypes property of the variable be compatible with the type of the value class used. The simplest way to ensure this is to equate the type of the value class with the name of the class. Two aggregations create the pair: PolicyVariableInSimplePolicyCondition relates a simple condition to a single variable instance, and PolicyValueInSimplePolicyCondition relates it to a single value instance. The variable and value instances may already exist as reusable objects in a ReusablePolicyContainer.

The MATCH operator is overloaded. In DestinationPort MATCH '80' the interpretation is equality. In DestinationPort MATCH {'80', '8080'} it is IS SET MEMBER. In DestinationPort MATCH {'1 to 255'} it is IN INTEGER RANGE. In SourceIPAddress MATCH 'MyCompany.com' it is IP ADDRESS AS RESOLVED BY DNS. The interpretation is always derived from the bound variable and the value instance. Generic rules cover the cases of a singleton, a range and a set, independently of the type: a singleton matching a range is true if it matches the lower bound, the upper bound or a value in between; a range matching a range is true if all of its values are in the other range, so [3..5] matches [1..6] is true while [3..5] matches [4..6] is false; and a range matching a set is true if all the values in the range are part of the set.

Variables are of two kinds. An explicitly bound variable has its value given in the condition. An implicitly bound variable is bound by the context, for example by the flow being conditioned, and 21 subclasses are defined in PCIMe, covering source and destination IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, source and destination ports, the IP protocol, the IP version, the IP type of service and DSCP, the flow identifier, source and destination MAC addresses, the VLAN identifier, the class of service, the Ethernet type, the source and destination service access points, the SNAP OUI and type, and the flow direction. Seven value subclasses are defined as well, for IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses, strings, bit strings, integers and booleans.

PCIMe contains two mechanisms for representing packet filters. The more general, the domain-level model, expresses packet filters in terms of policy variables and policy values. The other, the device-level model, expresses packet filters in a way that maps more directly to the packet fields the filters apply to. It is possible to map between the two representations, but no mapping is provided in PCIMe itself.

For domain-level filtering, each simple policy condition represents a single field to be filtered on, such as the source IP address, the destination IP address or the source port, and an additional simple condition indicates the direction the packet is travelling on the interface, inbound or outbound. Because of that condition, care must be taken when aggregating simple conditions into a CompoundFilterCondition, or the result may match all inbound packets, or all outbound packets, when that is probably not intended. Individual simple conditions may be negated when they are aggregated. CompoundFilterCondition is a subclass of CompoundPolicyCondition and adds one property, the boolean IsMirrored, which allows a single compound filter to match packets travelling in both directions on a higher-level connection such as a TCP session. When it is TRUE, additional packets match the filter: with a filter requiring direction In, source IP 9.1.1.1 and source port 80, an outbound packet also matches if its destination IP is 9.1.1.1 and its destination port is 80. IsMirrored flips the flow direction, the source and destination IP addresses, the source and destination ports, the source and destination MAC addresses, and the source and destination layer 2 service access points.

At the device level, packet header filters are represented by two subclasses of the abstract class FilterEntryBase, IpHeadersFilter and 8021Filter, and submodels may define others. Instances of these subclasses are not used directly as filters; they are always aggregated into a FilterList through the EntriesInFilterList aggregation, where the EntrySequence property always takes its default value of 0, meaning the entries are ANDed together. The FilterList class has an enumeration property Direction, and the value Mirrored(4) means exactly what IsMirrored means in a compound filter condition.
sections.plainLanguage: A simple condition compares one thing with another, such as the source port with 80, and the memo fixes what that comparison means for each kind of value. Actions work the other way round and set a value. For filtering packets there are two ways to write it: the general way, using those variables, or the device way, using a class that holds every field of a header at once. The device way is more direct; the memo does not define a way to convert between the two.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Policy Core Information Model of RFC 3060 describes the general security considerations related to the general core policy model, and the extensions defined in this document do not introduce any additional considerations related to security.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds nothing new on security. The security considerations of the model it extends are the ones that apply.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT CHANGES LISTED IN RFC 3460

items.title: PolicyRepository retired
items.text: Replaced by ReusablePolicyContainer, which can hold any reusable policy element.

items.title: Richer containment
items.text: PolicySetComponent lets a group contain a group and a rule contain a rule.

items.title: Priorities move
items.text: The Priority property leaves PolicyRule and moves onto the containment relationship.

items.title: Decision strategies
items.text: FirstMatching and AllMatching say how the rules in a set are evaluated.

items.title: Roles grow
items.text: PolicyRoles moves up to PolicySet, and a new class ties roles to resources.

items.title: Compound elements
items.text: Compound conditions and actions, with DNF or CNF conditions and ordered actions.

items.title: Variables and values
items.text: A simple condition matches a variable against a value; a simple action sets one.

items.title: Packet filters
items.text: Domain-level filters over header fields, and device-level filter classes.
